source: Shen et al. (2026) Can Vision-Language Models Analyze Human-Centered Video?
finding: A general VLM annotates human video close to human level on average. Human checking of VLM output is best and cheaper than human-alone.
numbers: 15 tasks from open datasets; VLM-alone mean HNS 97.0 (human=100); VLM+human verification 121.5; human time -48.9%; cost -31.3% to -44.5%. Based on 1,702 CHI 2026 papers, 125 annotate video.
limits: Single VLM (gemini-3.7-flash); 15 tasks; HNS normalised to chance and human.
agent_relevance: Video coding is the core cognitive-ethnography method. Draft-then-verify beats either alone: a pattern for an agent loop.

source: Shen et al. (2026) VLM video analysis, task-level results
finding: VLM accuracy varies hugely by phenomenon. It beats humans on interface actions, workflow reconstruction, gesture and intent. It fails on attention and mental-state cues.
numbers: Attentional orientation HNS 17.8; mistake handling 47.0; isolated sign recognition 35.4; interactional dominance 82.9; workflow reconstruction 118.2; communicative intent 134.0; co-speech gesture 128.4; interface events 106.9.
limits: Attention coding result may be partly bounding-box noise (authors' note).
agent_relevance: Models are good at what happened (steps) and weak at what someone attended to or believed. Do not trust them for inferred mental state without checking.

source: Shen et al. (2026) VLM video analysis, verification effects
finding: Human verification helps most where the VLM is weak and can hurt where the VLM is already accurate.
numbers: Attention coding 17.8 -> 140.1; mistake handling 47.0 -> 113.8; sign recognition 35.4 -> 100.0; but behavior interval 101.6 -> 86.5; animal behavior 110.8 -> 90.5. Human-human agreement rose on 11 of 15 tasks (workflow 0.761 -> 0.925; outcome/breakdown 0.680 -> 0.760).
limits: Verifiers may over-edit correct output.
agent_relevance: Route checking by task type: verify weak categories, skip it for precise categories the model already does well.

source: Shen et al. (2026) VLM video analysis, cost
finding: Machine coding of video is very cheap.
numbers: Whole benchmark cost $16.03 for 1,459 API requests over 895.7 minutes of video; $1.07 per hour of video; VLM-alone 82.4% to 95.6% cheaper than human-alone.
limits: Cost model assumes $5 to $20 hourly labor.
agent_relevance: Cheap enough to code every hour of a long agent trace, not a sample.

source: Shen et al. (2026) taxonomy of video-annotation practice in CHI 2026
finding: Survey of how HCI researchers annotate video: most use automatic annotation, but 44% still use researcher or expert annotation.
numbers: 125 of 1,702 CHI 2026 papers annotate video; external scene view 56.0%, egocentric 37.6%, screen recordings 11.2%; automatic annotation 58.4%, expert 44.0%, participant 4.0%; most common reasoning task local temporal 47.2%.
limits: Counts overlap across categories.
agent_relevance: Shows where the method sits in current practice: video, local timing judgments, increasingly machine-labelled.

source: Gilardi, Alizadeh, Kubli (2023) ChatGPT outperforms crowd-workers for text annotation
finding: Zero-shot ChatGPT beats MTurk crowd workers on tweet and news annotation and is more self-consistent.
numbers: n=6,183 items over 4 datasets; ChatGPT zero-shot accuracy about 25 points above crowd-workers on average; intercoder agreement above both crowd and trained annotators on all tasks; under $0.003 per annotation, about 30x cheaper than MTurk.
limits: Accuracy is measured against trained annotators; text only; 2023 model.
agent_relevance: LLM coding of field notes and transcripts is feasible at scale; agreement across runs is a usable reliability check.

source: Toernberg (2023) ChatGPT-4 outperforms experts and crowd workers
finding: GPT-4 labels political tweets with higher accuracy and reliability than experts and crowd, including items needing context and author intent.
numbers: LLM beat all individual human classifiers; plurality of 10 MTurk workers beat experts and the LLM was slightly above that; low temperature gave slightly higher accuracy and lower spread.
limits: One task type (US political tweets).
agent_relevance: Inference about intent, a hard part of ethnographic coding, is within reach for text. Use low temperature for coding.

source: Toernberg (2023) and Gilardi et al. (2023) shared limits for LLM coding
finding: Both studies score the model against labelled benchmarks; neither tests dense field video or interpretive ethnographic coding.
numbers: Gilardi n=6,183 texts; Toernberg one political tweet task.
limits: Benchmark accuracy is not interpretive validity.
agent_relevance: Do not read these results as proof that models can do deep ethnographic interpretation.

source: Zhang et al. (2023) QualiGPT: GPT as an easy-to-use tool for qualitative coding
finding: A structured-prompt GPT tool for thematic coding captured the main themes of manual coding and gave quotes and justifications for each theme.
numbers: Compared to manual coding on simulated and real data; themes in a table with quotes and participant counts; user picks number of themes. No kappa reported in the text read.
limits: Qualitative comparison only; small datasets.
agent_relevance: Quote-backed, justified themes let a human verify cheaply. Same rule fits agent claims: cite the source.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Redefining qualitative analysis in the AI era: ChatGPT for thematic analysis
finding: Researchers found ChatGPT thematic analysis erratic until given a structured prompt framework.
numbers: 17 interview participants plus 13 qualitative researchers co-designed a prompt framework: task and method description, background, output format as core; data structure, role-play and friendly wording as extras.
limits: Interview and design study; no accuracy numbers on theme quality.
agent_relevance: Prompt structure matters for coding reliability; main concerns were transparency and verifiability.

source: Gao et al. (2023) CollabCoder: LLM-assisted collaborative qualitative analysis
finding: A three-phase tool (independent open coding, discussion with Cohen's kappa and agreement rate, code groups) adds LLM suggestions to team coding.
numbers: Three phases; kappa and agreement rate shown live; users found kappa useful for finding disagreement (P9).
limits: Small user study; no accuracy numbers recorded here.
agent_relevance: Mirrors human inter-rater workflow; an agent could code independently several times, compute kappa, then reconcile.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
finding: An LLM agent with memory stream, reflection and planning produced more believable behavior than crowdworkers role-playing the same agents.
numbers: TrueSkill mu: full 29.89; no reflection 26.88; no reflection or planning 25.64; crowdworkers 22.95; no memory, planning, reflection 21.21; full vs baseline d=8.16; Kruskal-Wallis H(4)=150.29, p<0.001; 100 evaluators.
limits: Believability is judged by raters.
agent_relevance: Each architecture part adds value. Memory plus reflection is a cognitive-model pipeline relevant to the schema.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents, emergent social diffusion
finding: Over two simulated days information spread through the community without user steering, like information flow in a workplace.
numbers: Knowledge of mayoral candidacy 1 to 8 agents of 25 (4% to 32%); party knowledge 1 to 13 (4% to 52%); network density 0.167 to 0.74; 12 agents in one invitation path.
limits: 25 agents, one sandbox.
agent_relevance: Distributed information flow can be simulated and measured: a testbed for observation methods.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents, memory limits and failure modes
finding: Authors report failures: retrieval gets harder as memory grows, agents embellish memories, and agents drift from norms.
numbers: 6 of 453 awareness answers hallucinated (1.3%); some agents chose a lunch location by crowd convergence.
limits: Mostly described in text, not systematically measured.
agent_relevance: Boundary conditions for memory-based observers: retrieval at scale and embellishment.

source: Park et al. (2024) Generative Agent Simulations of 1,000 People
finding: Agents built from two-hour interview transcripts predict people's survey answers.
numbers: 1,052 Americans; interview-only agents 83%, survey-only 82%, combined 86% of participants' own test-retest accuracy.
limits: Normalised to participants' self-consistency.
agent_relevance: Ethnographic-style interview data is richer fuel for models than demographic labels.

source: Hong et al. (2024) MetaGPT: Meta Programming for a Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework
finding: Encoding human team SOPs, role specialisation and a shared message pool (publish/subscribe) beat free chat between agents.
numbers: HumanEval 85.9% and MBPP 87.7% Pass@1; SoftwareDev executability 3.75 of 4 vs ChatDev 2.25; run time 503 s vs 762 s (no-feedback variant); 124.3 tokens per line vs 248.9 for ChatDev.
limits: Authors' own SoftwareDev benchmark.
agent_relevance: A Hutchins-style shared artifact (message pool, structured outputs) as coordination medium beats open conversation.

source: Qian et al. (2023) ChatDev: Communicative Agents for Software Development
finding: Role-played software company following a waterfall chat chain; its own table compares to GPT-Engineer and MetaGPT.
numbers: ChatDev completeness 0.5600, executability 0.8800, consistency 0.8021, quality 0.3953 vs MetaGPT quality 0.1523 (in ChatDev's table).
limits: Conflicts with MetaGPT's own table; each paper picks its own benchmark.
agent_relevance: Multi-agent comparisons depend on the author's benchmark; treat with care.

source: Han and Zhang (2025) LLM multi-agent systems based on blackboard architecture
finding: A shared blackboard where agents are chosen by board content, repeated until consensus, beats fixed and static multi-agent baselines.
numbers: Six benchmarks (MMLU 1,140 q, ARC-C, GPQA-Diamond, BBH date, MATH 500, GSM8K); +4.33% average over CoT and +5.02% over static multi-agent methods.
limits: Small benchmark subsets.
agent_relevance: Blackboard is an old AI form of distributed cognition (shared visible workspace); modern tests show a modest gain.

source: Shang et al. (2026) United Minds or Isolated Agents? CoThinker under Cognitive Load Theory
finding: Specialised agents plus a shared collective working memory help on reasoning-heavy tasks and not on light ones.
numbers: Holm-corrected paired bootstrap: Data analysis +16.2% norm (+5.3 pp) vs IO, p<.001; Reasoning +15.5% vs CoT (+5.1 pp), p=0.001; Language +18.3% vs SR (+6.0 pp); instruction following about -1.2 pp vs IO (no gain).
limits: Gains concentrate where intrinsic load is high; overhead dominates on easy tasks.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: distribute cognition only when the task is hard; coordination has a cost.

source: Venkatesh and Cui (2026) Do Agent Societies Develop Intellectual Elites?
finding: Large-scale event-level trace analysis of LLM multi-agent systems, a quantitative form of observing cognition in the wild: coordination cascades are heavy-tailed and concentrate in a few agents.
numbers: Over 1.5 million interactions; power laws favoured over log-normal and exponential; scaling exponents between 2 and 3; integration bottleneck (expansion grows with size, consolidation does not); Deficit-Triggered Integration improves task success most where imbalance is largest.
limits: Own tasks and topologies; DTI effect sizes not extracted.
agent_relevance: Instrumenting agent traces like fieldwork finds structure; forced consolidation steps fix the bottleneck.

source: Liu, Arumugam, Zhang, Escola, Pitkow, Griffiths (2026) Cognitive Models and AI Algorithms Provide Templates for Designing Language Agents
finding: Position paper: formalises an agent template as a directed acyclic graph of LLM roles and surveys language agents derived from cognitive models.
numbers: No new experiments in the part read.
limits: Position paper; evidence is survey based.
agent_relevance: Supports building the schema from named cognitive templates.

source: Beyond Static Responses: Multi-Agent LLM Systems as a New Paradigm for Social Science Research (2025)
finding: Position paper states multi-agent LLM configurations mirror distributed-cognition principles (knowledge spread across agents and artifacts).
numbers: Conceptual claim; cites Zhang and Patel on distributed cognition; no test.
limits: Skimmed by keyword search only; no empirical measures.
agent_relevance: Distributed cognition is used as a metaphor in 2025 LLM work and rarely tested.

source: Hutchins 2024 Paris IAS project: Distributed Cognition and Cognitive Ethnography Meet Generative AI
finding: A secondary source reports Hutchins began a 2024 project joining cognitive ethnography with generative AI. No outputs found.
numbers: None.
limits: Secondary field-guide text seen only in search results; no primary paper found.
agent_relevance: The method's founder is now looking at LLMs; watch for outputs.

source: Search negative result: no study applies Hutchins-style cognitive ethnography to LLM agent teams
finding: In arXiv and web searches I found no direct ethnographic study of LLM agent coordination in the Hutchins tradition.
numbers: Zero direct hits across 6 web and arXiv queries; OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were rate-limited.
limits: Absence of evidence under limited search.
agent_relevance: Open niche: apply the method to our own agent traces (see Venkatesh and Cui).

source: Sumers et al. (2023) Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)
finding: Proposes memory, action space and a decision loop as an organising frame for language agents.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Seen in search listing only.
agent_relevance: Reference frame for relating schema operators to cognitive architectures.

source: Xiao et al. (2023) Supporting Qualitative Analysis with LLMs: codebook with GPT-3 for deductive coding
finding: Recalled, not verified: putting the codebook in the prompt gave usable agreement with experts for deductive coding.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers.
limits: Unverified; do not rely on it.
agent_relevance: Candidate to open next.
